subject: Accounting
title: The Global Minimum Tax
description: A 60-second lesson on The Global Minimum Tax.

hook.text: In 2021, 136 countries agreed on a global minimum corporate tax of 15%. A historic first.

buildup.text: The OECD brokered the deal to stop the race to the bottom in corporate tax rates.

discovery.text: If a company pays less than 15% anywhere, its home country can top up the tax to reach the minimum.

twist.text: Implementation is messy—countries interpret the rules differently and some drag their feet.

climax.text: The minimum tax could generate $150 billion in additional revenue globally each year.

punchline.text: A floor under tax rates. The world finally agreed on one.

quiz.question: What is the agreed global minimum corporate tax rate?

details.summary: The global minimum tax, agreed by over 130 countries in 2021, sets a 15% floor on corporate taxation worldwide, aimed at ending the race to the bottom where countries compete by offering ever-lower tax rates to attract multinational corporations.
details.whyItMatters: The global minimum tax represents the most significant international tax reform in a century, fundamentally changing how multinational corporations are taxed and reducing the incentive for profit shifting.
takeaways: Over 130 countries agreed to a 15% minimum corporate tax rate under the OECD's Pillar Two framework
If a company pays less than 15% in any country, its home country can collect the difference
The reform targets large multinationals with over €750 million in global revenue

faq.question: How does the global minimum tax work?
faq.answer: Under the OECD's Pillar Two framework, if a multinational corporation pays an effective tax rate below 15% in any country, its home country can impose a top-up tax to bring the rate to 15%. This removes the incentive for companies to shift profits to zero-tax jurisdictions.

faq.question: Does the global minimum tax eliminate tax havens?
faq.answer: It doesn't eliminate them but significantly reduces their appeal. Countries can still offer rates below 15%, but the tax savings disappear because the company's home country will collect the difference. This reduces the incentive for profit shifting while allowing countries to set their own rates.
